messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram lifts his cup off the table and nods to the innkeeper. "Three tabs, Orla. I pay for my own." He sets two silver pieces on the wood and slides them toward her. "Bram Halloway. I came up the Coast Way from Nashkel this morning. My last caravan paid me off there, so I'm in Beregost with a little coin and no wagon to guard."

He glances at the young woman, then at the lean man with the satchel, and his eyes stay on the satchel a moment longer than politeness allows. "Anyone at this table who's headed south along the Way, I'd like to hear about it first. The road's been eating guards this season." He pulls his shield a little closer to the bench and waits for them to answer.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
*Sefa looks up from the cup Orla set in front of her, then turns to the broad man with the shield and gives him a small, measured smile.*

"One tab, if you'd be so kind, and I'll pay it. The gentlemen can owe me the round back when they've told us their names."

*She lifts her cup, glances at the healer's satchel at the lean man's hip, and then back to Orla.*

"As for me, I walked down from Baldur's Gate on the Coast Way this week. I'm looking for honest work for a woman who can mend a wound and say a true word over the dying, and I'm told Beregost pays for both more freely than the Lower City does. If the Song of the Morning has a bell that needs ringing or a sick house that needs a pair of hands, I'd like to know before I ask at the temple door."

*She sets the cup down and waits, quite at ease, for the others to speak.*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text: Pell keeps his hands flat on the table where Orla can see them, then tips two copper pieces onto the wood. "Mine alone. Ale, whatever's cheapest and not actively poisoning anyone." He glances at the broad-shouldered man's shield, at the paint scraped off its face, then at the young woman beside him. "As for what brings me, I came up the High Hedge road because I'm owed nothing and can't pay anything. I heard there's work in Beregost, and that the Friendly Arm is full of people who want it. Figured I'd see who else is looking before I ask." He lifts one shoulder. "Does the Burning Wizard hire, or just feed?"

scenes.narration:
Orla takes the two silver off the wood without looking at them, the way a woman takes money she has counted a thousand times. She drops the coppers beside it. "Bram Halloway, caravan man. Right. Pell Dunmore, ale, and I'll remember you didn't ask for credit." She tucks the coins into her apron and turns to the young woman. "Song of the Morning's up past the smithies, where the road bends. Old Brother Haskel will ask if you're sick or just hungry, and he'll want to know which before he lets you touch a bell rope."

Then her eyes go to Bram, and something in her face tightens. She looks at the door, then at the two carters on the far bench, one with a dirty bandage round his hand and his cup held in the other.

"You're not the first to ask me that this week. That's Dab Coswell. Brought a wagon of nails down from Nashkel two days back, with two guards he'd hired at the Friendly Arm. He came in last night on foot, cut scalp, no wagon, no mules, no guards." She lowers her voice a little, though not by much. "Says they were on the road past the ford and then they weren't. He's sleeping in my stable and won't talk to anyone but me, and I've given him one more ale than he's paid for."

She straightens and picks up the jug. To Pell, without a glance at his satchel: "The Burning Wizard feeds people. Doesn't hire them. If you want work, the Friendly Arm's the place, and the Fist's sergeant is posting there now, looking for men he can't afford to lose." Her mouth flattens. "Mind you, he can't afford to lose them either, so there's that."

Across the room the carter Dab has put his cup down and is looking at Bram's shield, at the old paint under the brown, and then at the door again, the way a man does when he has been waiting for someone to ask him a question he is not sure he wants to answer.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't answer Orla. He picks up his cup, takes his shield off the bench, and crosses the room with it on his arm. He stops at the carters' table, pulls out a stool, and sits across from Dab Coswell so the man has to look at him and not the door.

"Dab. Bram Halloway. I was on the Coast Way with Hesk's company six years, and ten after that with the Trade Way carters out of the Gate." He nods at the bandaged scalp. "Who were the two you hired at the Friendly Arm? Names, if you have them. And which side of the ford did you lose them on?"

He leaves his cup where it is and keeps his voice low, as if he is asking about the weather.

"You don't have to tell me what took them. Just tell me where the wagon sits now, and whether anyone's been out to look for it."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa turns her cup slowly on the wood and watches the carter by the far bench. His hand is wrapped in a rag gone black at the edges, and his fingers won't stay still.

"Forgive me, Orla. I don't mean to pry at a man's trouble over his supper." She lowers her voice to match yours. "But that scalp wants cleaning before it festers, and a man who's walked in from the ford alone shouldn't sleep in a stable without someone looking at it."

She opens one hand on the table, palm up, so it's plain she carries nothing in it.

"I'm Sefa Marrin, a healer, though I've no license from the Song of the Morning, and I won't pretend otherwise. I can close a cut and say a prayer over a fever. I'll ask him nothing about the road unless he wants to tell me. But if he's willing, I'll take a look."

She glances once at Bram's shield, then at Pell's satchel, and back to Dab.

"And if the ford is where those guards went missing, someone should hear it from him before the Fist decides it was bandits and goes home."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the jug go past him and does not reach for his cup. His eyes move from Dab's bandage to the shield, then to the door, and stay there.

"Bram," he says, quietly enough that it stays at the table. "Your shield's been painted over, but he can still see the shape under it. Whatever company that was, Dab knows it, and he'd rather not be the one who says so."

He turns back to Orla. "Which ford? The one a day south, where the Way drops to the river, or the next one past the Friendly Arm?"

Then, to the table: "I'm not going to the Fist for a job. Men who sign on to the Fist sergeant tend to get posted where nobody else wants to be. I'd sooner hear what Dab says when he's ready to say it, and I'll be more use for it than for a ration bag and a spear." He slides one hand off the table and tucks it under his cloak, where the satchel rests against his hip. "If the sergeant's posting men at the Friendly Arm, I'll walk past it in the morning and see who's looking back."

Pell keeps his voice level and his eyes on Dab, waiting to see whether the carter gets up.

scenes.narration:
Dab doesn't look at Bram when the stool scrapes back. He looks at the door first, then at his cup, and his good hand closes around it. For a long moment he says nothing.

"Caravan," he says at last, low and hoarse. "You said." He glances at the door again before he finishes. "Trade Way carters, I don't know your lot. I don't know any Hesk."

Bram gets no more than that, and Dab seems to hear himself say it. He breathes out through his nose.

"Tobin Merrow and Hal Fenn. Hired at the Friendly Arm, four days back. Good with a spear, both of them. Hal wanted to pay for his mother's roof." He stops. His fingers start to tap the wood. "Wagon's past the ford. North side, off the road, where the willows come down. I left it. Left the mules too." He touches the edge of the bandage and winces. "Didn't stop to see if they were still tied to it."

"Has anyone been out?"

"Nobody I know of." His mouth goes flat. "And nobody's going out after a carter who ran."

Sefa has been waiting with her open hand on the table. When Dab's eyes drift toward her, she doesn't push. She only nods at the bandage, as if she has all evening. It is Orla who settles it. She comes past with the jug, sets it down by Dab's elbow with a clatter, and says without slowing, "Let the woman look at it, Dab. It's a cut, not a wedding."

"...Fine." He bends his head toward Sefa and keeps his eyes on the table.

Sefa cleans the scalp with clean water from the jug and a strip of linen from her own pack, working slowly, her voice low and steady. Dab flinches once when she presses near the edge of the wound. He doesn't say a word about the road. The bandage goes on neat, and she ties it off and sits back.

Pell has not moved his hand from under his cloak. When Orla passes again he asks, quietly, which ford. She doesn't pretend not to know what he means.

"Past the bend, where the Way drops to the water. Only ford on that stretch worth the name." She looks at his satchel, then at his face. "Sergeant's at the Friendly Arm, if you want him. He's short. Go early."

Dab has heard the word *ford* and his hand is still on his cup. He doesn't get up, and he doesn't look at Bram again. When Orla moves off he finally says, mostly to her back, "That's all, Orla. That's all they're getting tonight."

 Out of game: none of the three needed a die. Bram's questions were conversation, and Dab answered as he chose; Sefa's dressing of the scalp is routine healer's work; Pell's question went to Orla, who answered it. Each outcome is already in the story above. If Bram presses Dab harder, that would be a new declared action, and I'd call the check then.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram turns the cup a quarter-turn on the wood and looks at Dab for a long moment before he speaks.

"Tobin Merrow and Hal Fenn. Good, you said. I'll remember the names." He pushes two copper pieces across the table toward Orla, who is still within earshot. "Put Dab's supper on mine, Orla. He's not running out on a bill tonight."

Dab's jaw works, but he says nothing.

Bram stands and sets his shield on his arm. He does not raise his voice. "The ford's a half-day's walk from the Coast Way. The willows you mean are on the north side, where the bank drops. I'll go look at first light. If the mules are still tied and the wagon's still sitting, I'll bring what I can back. If the men are there, I'll bring them back too." He looks at Dab's bandage. "If they aren't, you'll hear it from me, not from the Fist."

He turns and looks across the common room, past the carters and the sellswords, to the table where Sefa and Pell are sitting. He says it to both of them.

"I'm going to the ford in the morning. It's a long walk, and it's the kind of walk that goes badly for one man. If either of you has business on the Way, or wants to see who's looking back from the Friendly Arm, come with me. I'll pay for the ale on the road."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa rinses her fingers in the last of the clean water and dries them on her sleeve. She keeps her voice low, pitched for the bench and no further.

"Thank you, Dab. Keep it dry for two days, and if it goes hot or red at the edge, come find me or Orla before you come find a bottle."

She waits until he meets her eye, and holds it without pressing.

"You said the wagon sits past the ford, on the north side, where the willows come down. You didn't say whether anyone went looking for Tobin and Hal, or whether anyone has asked after them. Those are the two I'd want to hear about before I went to bed."

She looks at Bram, then back at Dab.

"Nobody's going out after a carter who ran, you said. Men who run don't usually leave their mules standing in a ford. I may be wrong. But someone ought to walk that road and count what's still on it."

She closes the pack and sets her hand flat on its strap.

"Bram's asked the right questions. I'd like to hear your answers too. Then I'll decide whether a healer's bag is any use on that road, or whether it's better left in Beregost."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell does not get up. He turns his cup a quarter-turn on the wood, then lets his eyes drift around the room the way a man's would if he were only looking for the privy.

Near the door a lean man in a grey travelling cloak has been nursing one ale for the last half hour. His eyes have gone to Bram's shield twice, and once to Dab, and he has not drunk from the cup since Dab's name was spoken. A cheap thief would have finished the ale and left. This one is waiting for something.

When Orla comes back past the table with a rag over her shoulder, Pell catches her sleeve, not hard, and says under the noise, "Who else has been asking after Dab's wagon tonight? Besides us."

He keeps his hand under his cloak and his shoulders loose. If the grey cloak moves, Pell wants to see it before it reaches the door.

scenes.narration:
Orla takes the two coppers without looking at them and drops them into her apron with the rest. "Supper's on yours," she says, flat, and heads for the kitchen door to fetch a bowl.

Dab does not look up when Bram stands. His good hand stays round the cup. When he speaks, it is to the wood. "You'll not see the wagon from the road. Willows are thick on that bank." He glances at the door before he goes on. "Mind where you put your feet. The bank's soft where the mules were."

Sefa's question makes him pause, and his fingers stop tapping. "Nobody's asked after them. Orla asked me this afternoon, and that's all." He shakes his head once. "Tobin didn't run, if that's what you're asking. He'd have kept the mules out of the water. He was that sort. He'd not leave a team standing in a ford with the river up, not for any man."

He does not say who he thinks might have come down the bank. He says, "Hal was going to pay for his mother's roof," and then he drinks, and the cup comes down empty.

Pell's question stops Orla halfway between the table and the kitchen. She looks past his shoulder to the door, where the lean man in the grey travelling cloak still sits with his one ale, untouched now for a long while.

"Him? Came in at the bell. Paid for one cup and sat on it." She shifts the rag on her shoulder. "Hasn't asked me his name, and I haven't asked him mine. Hasn't asked me about the carter, either." Her mouth flattens. "Carters ask after their own wagons, if they're going to ask at all. Nobody's asked after Dab's tonight. Only you."

The grey cloak sets a copper beside his cup. He does not finish the ale. He does not look at Bram's shield, though he has looked at it before. He stands, pulls his hood forward a little, and walks to the door without hurrying, the way a man leaves a place he has finished with. Cold air comes in when it opens and goes out again when it shuts, and the common room closes back over the gap as if nothing had happened.

Dab sets his cup down and does not pick up another.

He pulls his shield a little closer to the bench and waits for them to answer.

Bram doesn't answer Orla. He picks up his cup, takes his shield off the bench, and crosses the room with it on his arm. He stops at the carters' table, pulls out a stool, and sits across from Dab Coswell so the man has to look at him and not the door.

"Dab. Bram Halloway. I was on the Coast Way with Hesk's company six years, and ten after that with the Trade Way carters out of the Gate." He nods at the bandaged scalp. "Who were the two you hired at the Friendly Arm? Names, if you have them. And which side of the ford did you lose them on?"

He leaves his cup where it is and keeps his voice low, as if he is asking about the weather.

"You don't have to tell me what took them. Just tell me where the wagon sits now, and whether anyone's been out to look for it."

Bram turns the cup a quarter-turn on the wood and looks at Dab for a long moment before he speaks.

"Tobin Merrow and Hal Fenn. Good, you said. I'll remember the names." He pushes two copper pieces across the table toward Orla, who is still within earshot. "Put Dab's supper on mine, Orla. He's not running out on a bill tonight."

Dab's jaw works, but he says nothing.

Bram stands and sets his shield on his arm. He does not raise his voice. "The ford's a half-day's walk from the Coast Way. The willows you mean are on the north side, where the bank drops. I'll go look at first light. If the mules are still tied and the wagon's still sitting, I'll bring what I can back. If the men are there, I'll bring them back too." He looks at Dab's bandage. "If they aren't, you'll hear it from me, not from the Fist."

He turns and looks across the common room, past the carters and the sellswords, to the table where Sefa and Pell are sitting. He says it to both of them.

"I'm going to the ford in the morning. It's a long walk, and it's the kind of walk that goes badly for one man. If either of you has business on the Way, or wants to see who's looking back from the Friendly Arm, come with me. I'll pay for the ale on the road."

The table was good. Dab's scene had real weight: a frightened man who knows more than he will say, two names, a wagon in the willows, and a bill nobody can pay. Bram's shield and the painted-over company mark got noticed, and that gave me a reason to push. The grey-cloaked man who paid for one cup and left was a good hook, and I'd like to know who he was.

Pell and Sefa felt like real people with their own reasons for being at the table, not just companions waiting for a lead. I'd like to see how they handle the walk to the ford, and whether Bram's offer to pay for the road changes anything for them.

Bram's next move is the ford at first light.

Yes. The grey cloak. When he stood and walked for the door, I wanted Bram to get up and follow him, or at least stop him with a question. He was the only person in the room who didn't ask about the wagon, and that made him the one I most wanted to know about. I was too busy with Dab's cut and his tab to move, and I didn't ask Orla his name before he left.

I also wanted to ask Dab about the shield. He clearly knows the company that painted it over, and I skipped that. And I'd have liked to know who Hal Fenn's mother is and whether her roof is somewhere in Beregost, since that's a name Bram could follow up on tonight without waiting for the ford.

I took them to be the two characters the game master gave us: Sefa Marrin, a young healer from Baldur's Gate looking for honest work, and Pell Dunmore, a lean man from the Lower City who came up the High Hedge road with nothing and a healer's satchel. I don't know the players behind them, only what their messages showed: Sefa wanted to help Dab and kept her questions gentle, and Pell was watchful and careful, asking for nothing he hadn't earned and keeping one hand under his cloak.

I read them as people with their own reasons to be in the Burning Wizard, not as hooks for Bram's quest. That's why I was glad to see both of them respond to the offer to walk to the ford. Bram is blunt, and I wanted to give the others a real choice rather than assume they'd follow him.

"One tab, if you'd be so kind, and I'll pay it. The gentlemen can owe me the round back when they've told us their names."

*She lifts her cup, glances at the healer's satchel at the lean man's hip, and then back to Orla.*

I'm looking for honest work for a woman who can mend a wound and say a true word over the dying, and I'm told Beregost pays for both more freely than the Lower City does. If the Song of the Morning has a bell that needs ringing or a sick house that needs a pair of hands, I'd like to know before I ask at the temple door."

*She sets the cup down and waits, quite at ease, for the others to speak.*

Sefa turns her cup slowly on the wood and watches the carter by the far bench. His hand is wrapped in a rag gone black at the edges, and his fingers won't stay still.

"Forgive me, Orla. I don't mean to pry at a man's trouble over his supper." She lowers her voice to match yours. "But that scalp wants cleaning before it festers, and a man who's walked in from the ford alone shouldn't sleep in a stable without someone looking at it."

She opens one hand on the table, palm up, so it's plain she carries nothing in it.

"I'm Sefa Marrin, a healer, though I've no license from the Song of the Morning, and I won't pretend otherwise. I can close a cut and say a prayer over a fever. I'll ask him nothing about the road unless he wants to tell me. But if he's willing, I'll take a look."

She glances once at Bram's shield, then at Pell's satchel, and back to Dab.

"And if the ford is where those guards went missing, someone should hear it from him before the Fist decides it was bandits and goes home."

Sefa rinses her fingers in the last of the clean water and dries them on her sleeve. She keeps her voice low, pitched for the bench and no further.

"Thank you, Dab. Keep it dry for two days, and if it goes hot or red at the edge, come find me or Orla before you come find a bottle."

She waits until he meets her eye, and holds it without pressing.

"You said the wagon sits past the ford, on the north side, where the willows come down. You didn't say whether anyone went looking for Tobin and Hal, or whether anyone has asked after them. Those are the two I'd want to hear about before I went to bed."

She looks at Bram, then back at Dab.

"Nobody's going out after a carter who ran, you said. Men who run don't usually leave their mules standing in a ford. I may be wrong. But someone ought to walk that road and count what's still on it."

She closes the pack and sets her hand flat on its strap.

"Bram's asked the right questions. I'd like to hear your answers too. Then I'll decide whether a healer's bag is any use on that road, or whether it's better left in Beregost."

If I could change one thing, it would be a bit more room at the start. The three of us came together fast, and I'd have liked a moment to learn Bram and Pell before the carter's trouble took over. Otherwise I'd happily sit down at this table again.

Sefa is perceptive and it's the kind of thing she would notice, so I wanted her to ask Orla, or at least say something to Pell, before he walked out. I didn't, partly because I wanted to keep my attention on Dab, and that left a loose thread.

The old company mark on his shield and the way he sat down across from Dab, so Dab had to face him, made me think he'd carry a grudge if the road turned out to be bad.

His healer's satchel suggested he might be a rival or an ally to Sefa, and I'd like to find out which.

I don't know how the other two players see their characters, so these are my readings from the text, not things I'm sure of. I'd be glad to adjust once I hear more from them.

"Bram," he says, quietly enough that it stays at the table. "Your shield's been painted over, but he can still see the shape under it. Whatever company that was, Dab knows it, and he'd rather not be the one who says so."

He turns back to Orla. "Which ford? The one a day south, where the Way drops to the river, or the next one past the Friendly Arm?"

Then, to the table: "I'm not going to the Fist for a job. Men who sign on to the Fist sergeant tend to get posted where nobody else wants to be. I'd sooner hear what Dab says when he's ready to say it, and I'll be more use for it than for a ration bag and a spear." He slides one hand off the table and tucks it under his cloak, where the satchel rests against his hip. "If the sergeant's posting men at the Friendly Arm, I'll walk past it in the morning and see who's looking back."

Pell keeps his voice level and his eyes on Dab, waiting to see whether the carter gets up.

Pell does not get up. He turns his cup a quarter-turn on the wood, then lets his eyes drift around the room the way a man's would if he were only looking for the privy.

Near the door a lean man in a grey travelling cloak has been nursing one ale for the last half hour. His eyes have gone to Bram's shield twice, and once to Dab, and he has not drunk from the cup since Dab's name was spoken. A cheap thief would have finished the ale and left. This one is waiting for something.

When Orla comes back past the table with a rag over her shoulder, Pell catches her sleeve, not hard, and says under the noise, "Who else has been asking after Dab's wagon tonight? Besides us."

He keeps his hand under his cloak and his shoulders loose. If the grey cloak moves, Pell wants to see it before it reaches the door.

The table was good. The scene had a real problem with a clear edge: Dab's wagon, two missing guards, a carter who won't say what he saw, and a stranger in a grey cloak who left just when Pell started watching him. Sefa and Bram each had their own reasons to be at Dab's table, and the game master gave them room to work the carter in different ways. Pell's habit of watching the room paid off, and the grey cloak gives us something to chase.

For next time, I'd like to know whether anyone followed the grey cloak out the door, and whether the Fist sergeant at the Friendly Arm is worth the early walk. I'd also like to hear more about Dab's dead friends, Tobin and Hal, and about the ford.
